items.title: Many-Valued Logic
items.description: [Revised entry by João Marcos, Adam Přenosil, and Paul Egré on September 29, 2026. Changes to: Main text, Bibliography] Many-valued logics, understood in the broadest sense, are systems of logic that generalize the two-valued truth-functional basis of classical logic to any number of truth values. All of these questions are highly controversial and have sparked heated debates, both philosophical and empirical, over the past few decades....

items.description: [Revised entry by Gwen Griffith-Dickson on September 23, 2026. Changes to: Main text, Bibliography] Johann Georg Hamann (1730 - 1788) lived and worked in Prussia, in the context of the late German Enlightenment. Although he remained outside 'professional' philosophical circles, in that he never held a University post, he was respected in his time for his scholarship and breadth of learning. His writings were notorious even in his own time for the challenges they threw down to the reader. These challenges to interpretation and understanding are only heightened today....

items.title: Aesthetics and Race
items.description: [New Entry by Monique Roelofs on September 22, 2026.] Aesthetics and race constitute areas of experience, evaluation, and historical practice that are vitally entangled with one another. items.title: Impartiality
items.description: [Revised entry by Troy Jollimore on September 17, 2026. Changes to: Main text, Bibliography] Impartiality is sometimes treated by philosophers as if it were equivalent to moral impartiality. Or, at the very least, the former word is often used, without the qualifying adjective 'moral', even when it is the particularly moral concept that is intended. This is potentially misleading, since impartiality in its broadest sense is best understood as a formal notion that can be applied in a number of contexts, including non-moral contexts....

items.title: Indexicals
items.description: [Revised entry by David Braun and Alexandru Radulescu on September 3, 2026. Changes to: Main text, Bibliography] An indexical is, roughly speaking, a linguistic expression whose reference can shift from context to context. For example, the indexical 'you' may refer to one person in one context and to another person in another context. Other paradigmatic examples of indexicals are 'I', 'here', 'today', 'yesterday', 'he', 'she', and 'that'. items.title: Ratnakīrti
items.description: [New Entry by Patrick McAllister on August 26, 2026.] Ratnakīrti was a Buddhist scholar at Vikramaśīla monastery during the first half of the eleventh century CE. Today, he is best known for ten philosophical works on metaphysical, epistemological, logical and Buddhological topics. These ten works have survived in their original language, Sanskrit.
